fetched_contents.text: Early Treatment with Prednisolone or Acyclovir in Bell's Palsy Abstract Background Corticosteroids and antiviral agents are widely used to treat the early stages of idiopathic facial paralysis (i.e., Bell's palsy), but their effectiveness is uncertain. Methods We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, factorial trial involving patients with Bell's palsy who were recruited within 72 hours after the onset of symptoms. Patients were randomly assigned to receive 10 days of treatment with prednisolone, acyclovir, both agents, or placebo. The primary outcome was recovery of facial function, as rated on the House–Brackmann scale. Secondary outcomes included quality of life, appearance, and pain. Results Final outcomes were assessed for 496 of 551 patients who underwent randomization. At 3 months, the proportions of patients who had recovered facial function were 83.0% in the prednisolone group as compared with 63.6% among patients who did not receive prednisolone (P<0.001) and 71.2% in the acyclovir group as compared with 75.7% among patients who did not receive acyclovir (adjusted P=0.50). After 9 months, these proportions were 94.4% for prednisolone and 81.6% for no prednisolone (P<0.001) and 85.4% for acyclovir and 90.8% for no acyclovir (adjusted P=0.10). For patients treated with both drugs, the proportions were 79.7% at 3 months (P<0.001) and 92.7% at 9 months (P<0.001). There were no clinically significant differences between the treatment groups in secondary outcomes. There were no serious adverse events in any group. Conclusions In patients with Bell's palsy, early treatment with prednisolone significantly improves the chances of complete recovery at 3 and 9 months. There is no evidence of a benefit of acyclovir given alone or an additional benefit of acyclovir in combination with prednisolone. (Current Controlled Trials number, ISRCTN71548196.) Bell's palsy is acute, idiopathic, unilateral paralysis of the facial nerve.1 Vascular, inflammatory, and viral causes have been suggested from paired serologic analyses and studies of the cerebral ganglia, suggesting an association between herpes infection and the onset of facial paralysis.2–4 Epidemiologic studies show that 11 to 40 persons per 100,000 are affected each year, most commonly between the ages of 30 and 45 years.5 Although most patients recover well, up to 30% of patients have a poor recovery, with continuing facial disfigurement, psychological difficulties, and facial pain.6,7 Treatment remains controversial and variable.8 Prednisolone and acyclovir are commonly prescribed separately and in combination, although evidence of their effectiveness is weak.9,10 Two recent Cochrane reviews assessed the effectiveness of corticosteroids and antiviral agents in patients with Bell's palsy. The analysis of corticosteroid treatment pooled the results of four randomized, controlled trials with a total of 179 patients.11 The review of antiviral treatment included three studies involving 246 patients.12 Both reviews independently concluded that insufficient data exist to support the use of either or both therapies. Given this lack of evidence, the Health Technology Assessment Program of the National Institute for Health Research commissioned an independent academic group to determine whether prednisolone or acyclovir used early in the course of Bell's palsy improves the chances of recovery.13 Methods Patients We established receiving centers at 17 hospitals throughout Scotland, to which potential patients with Bell's palsy were referred. Eligible patients with a confirmed diagnosis who consented to join the study were randomly assigned to study groups and were followed for 9 months. Complete details of the study design and the analysis plan have been published previously.14 The complete study protocol appears in the Supplementary Appendix, available with the full text of this article at www.nejm.org. We recruited adults 16 years of age or older with unilateral facial-nerve weakness of no identifiable cause who presented to primary care or the emergency department and could be referred to a collaborating otorhinolaryngologist within 72 hours after the onset of symptoms. Exclusion criteria were pregnancy, breast-feeding, uncontrolled diabetes (glycated hemoglobin level, >8%), peptic ulcer disease, suppurative otitis media, herpes zoster, multiple sclerosis, systemic infection, sarcoidosis and other rare conditions, and an inability to provide informed consent. All patients provided written informed consent after the aims and methods of the study had been described to them and after they had received an information sheet. The study was approved by the Multicenter Research Ethics Committee for Scotland and was conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. Drugs (including placebo) were purchased from Tayside Pharmaceuticals, an organization that manufactures special medicines for the National Health Service in Scotland and for commercial customers. fetched_contents.text: Bell Palsy Treatment & Management: Approach Considerations, Pharmacologic Therapy, Local Treatment Treatment Approach Considerations Because persons with true Bell palsy generally have an excellent prognosis, and because spontaneous recovery is fairly common, treatment of Bell palsy is still controversial. The goals of treatment are to improve facial nerve (seventh cranial nerve) function and reduce neuronal damage. Treatment of Bell palsy should be conservative and guided by the severity and probable prognosis in each particular case. Studies have shown the benefit of high-dose corticosteroids for acute cases. [44, 45] Although antiviral treatment has also come into use, evidence is now available indicating that it may not be beneficial. [44] (See Medication.) Topical ocular therapy is useful in most cases, with the exception of those in which the condition is severe or prolonged. In these cases, surgical management is best. Several procedures are aimed at protecting the cornea from exposure and achieving facial symmetry. These procedures reduce the need for constant use of lubrication drops or ointments, may improve cosmesis, and may be needed to preserve vision on the affected side. Many issues must be addressed in treating patients with Bell palsy. The most important is the onset of symptoms. Treatment may be considered for patients who present within 1–4 days of the onset of paralysis. Patients with Bell palsy frequently present to the emergency department (ED). The role of the ED clinician consists of the following: * Initiate appropriate treatment * Protect the eye * Arrange appropriate medical follow-up care The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) published a practice parameter in 2001 stating that steroids are probably effective and acyclovir (with prednisone) is possibly effective for the treatment of Bell palsy. There was insufficient evidence for recommendations on facial decompression surgery. [46] In 2012, the AAN released guidelines stating that steroids are highly likely to be effective and increase the likelihood of recovery of facial nerve function in new-onset Bell palsy [4, 6] Guidelines from the American Academy of Otolaryngology—Head and Neck Surgery Foundation also recommend the use of corticosteroids. [36] A variety of nonpharmacologic measures have been used to treat Bell palsy, including physical therapy (eg, facial exercises, [47] neuromuscular retraining [48] ) and acupuncture. [49] No adverse effects of these treatments have been reported. Reviews suggest that physical therapy may result in faster recovery and reduced sequelae, but further randomized, controlled trials are needed to confirm any benefit. Many patients with Bell palsy may have problems with eating or drinking, swallowing difficulty (overt or unrecognized), and speech disturbances caused by muscle weakness and associated facial asymmetry. Establishing the correct diagnosis is imperative and choosing the correct treatment options can optimise the likelihood of recovery. Objective This article summarises our understanding of Bell’s palsy and the evidence-based management options available for adult patients. Discussion The basic assessment should include a thorough history and physical examination as the diagnosis of Bell’s palsy is based on exclusion. For confirmed cases of Bell’s palsy, corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment and should be initiated within 72 hours of symptom onset. Antiviral therapy in combination with corticosteroid therapy may confer a small benefit and may be offered on the basis of shared decision making. Currently, no recommendations can be made for acupuncture, physical therapy, electrotherapy or surgical decompression because well-designed studies are lacking and available data are of low quality. Bell’s palsy is characterised by an acute onset of unilateral, lower motor neuron weakness of the facial nerve in the absence of an identifiable cause.1 The annual incidence is estimated to be 11–40 per 100,000, with a lifetime risk of one in 60. On average, general practitioners (GPs) encounter one acute case every two years.2 Most cases of Bell’s palsy resolve spontaneously. Indeed, 71% of patients notice clinical improvement within three weeks of symptom onset and achieve complete recovery within three months. The remainder of patients fail to recover completely and continue to have facial weakness, synkinesis and contractures. Facial dysfunction has a dramatic effect on a patient’s appearance, psychological wellbeing and quality of life.3 Management of Bell’s palsy is aimed at achieving complete recovery or reducing the negative sequelae in cases that fail to resolve. This article summarises our understanding of Bell’s palsy and the evidence-based management options available for adult patients. Case 1 Mr XY, 32 year of age, presents with a history of rapidly progressive, right-sided facial paralysis. Prior to this, he had been systemically well. Case 2 Mrs PL, 76 years of age, presents with progressive weakness of the left forehead muscles over the course of two weeks. Prior to this, she had been systemically well. How to diagnose Bell’s palsy The exact mechanism of Bell’s palsy is unknown, although a viral aetiology is suspected.1,2 The unilateral facial weakness associated with Bell’s palsy is thought to result from facial nerve inflammation and oedema induced by reactivation of Herpes simplex or Varicella zoster virus.1–3 In the temporal bone, the facial nerve travels in a narrow canal; swelling of the nerve may result in compression and subsequent damage. The facial nerve innervates the lacrimal glands, salivary glands, stapedius muscle, taste fibres from the anterior tongue, and general sensory fibres from the posterior ear canal and tympanic membrane. In addition to unilateral facial weakness, patients may report dryness of the eye and mouth, taste disturbance and hyperacusis. Specific risk factors for Bell’s palsy include pregnancy, severe pre-eclampsia, obesity, hypertension, diabetes and upper respiratory illnesses such as influenza. Diagnosis of Bell’s palsy is based on exclusion.1–3 The aim of a thorough history and physical examination is to exclude a neurological, otologic, infectious, inflammatory or neoplastic cause, as well as cerebellopontine angle pathology and vascular insufficiency (Box 1). The history should specifically enquire about the onset and timing of symptoms. Onset of Bell’s palsy is sudden, but not stroke-like, and tends to evolve over minutes to hours. Facial weakness often worsens while the patient is waiting in the emergency department. A strong mini-report on eye care, physical therapy, and other supportive treatments

Eye protection, eye drops, and artificial tears are central to managing Bell’s palsy because the condition often causes incomplete eye closure and corneal exposure. The evidence here explicitly states that “eye care is essential for patients with incomplete eye closure” and that topical ocular therapy is useful in most cases, with exceptions for severe or prolonged disease [N4-F3]. The Mayo Clinic source also notes that healthcare professionals may suggest “eye drops” as part of treatment to help speed recovery [N5-R1]. Medical News Today similarly explains how to use eye drops and eye-care strategies during recovery, emphasizing protection of the eye [N5-R4]. These treatments fit into the overall recovery picture as part of the supportive care bundle: they protect the cornea and reduce risk of complications, but they are not a substitute for corticosteroids or antivirals when indicated [N4-F3].

Physical therapy and facial massage are another key supportive approach. The Mayo Clinic states that “your healthcare professional may suggest medicines or physical therapy to help speed your recovery” [N5-R1], and the Medscape reference explicitly lists physical therapy as a nonpharmacologic measure, including facial exercises and neuromuscular retraining [N4-F3]. Medscape also notes that many issues in Bell’s palsy, such as eating, drinking, swallowing difficulty, and speech disturbance, may be addressed with occupational therapy and speech therapy assessments, with treatments that may improve clarity of speech, reduce dysphagia risks, and decrease social embarrassment [N4-F3]. However, the evidence status is important: reviews suggest that physical therapy may result in faster recovery and reduced sequelae, but further randomized, controlled trials are needed to confirm any benefit [N4-F3]. So the evidence supports physical therapy as part of recovery care, but it remains inconclusive as a standalone cure.

Acupuncture and other non-invasive therapies are mentioned in the evidence, but their support is weaker. Medscape explicitly states that acupuncture has been used but that “no adverse effects of these treatments have been reported” and that reviews suggest physical therapy may help, although more evidence is needed [N4-F3]. The search result for non-invasive therapies also notes that corticosteroids, antiviral drugs, physical therapy, and supportive measures are available treatment alternatives [N5-R3]. However, the evidence here is thin: the cited sources do not provide strong proof of acupuncture’s efficacy, and the Medscape reference is cautious about recommending it outside of evidence-based guidance [N4-F3]. Therefore, acupuncture should be framed as an adjunct or complementary option rather than a first-line treatment.

Overall, these supportive treatments fit into recovery as part of a broader management plan. Eye care is prioritized in patients with incomplete eye closure [N4-F3], physical therapy may help speed recovery and reduce sequelae [N4-F3], and non-invasive therapies such as acupuncture may be considered cautiously [N4-F3]. The evidence does not support them as replacements for corticosteroids or antivirals in the main therapeutic algorithm, but they can be helpful in preserving function, protecting the eye, and improving quality of life [N4-F3][N5-R4].
node_outputs.N8:
A strong mini-report on corticosteroid use in Bell’s palsy

Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment for Bell’s palsy, but the evidence on whether they are helpful is nuanced. The RACGP guidance says corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment and should be initiated within 72 hours of symptom onset [N6-F4]. Medscape similarly states that “studies have shown the benefit of high-dose corticosteroids for acute cases” and that steroids are “probably effective” and “highly likely to be effective” in new-onset Bell’s palsy, with strong consideration to optimize outcomes [N4-F3]. The NEJM RCT also found that early treatment with prednisolone significantly improved the chances of complete recovery at 3 and 9 months, supporting a role for corticosteroids in acute cases [N3-F2]. However, the same NEJM evidence also notes that corticosteroid and antiviral treatment remains controversial because most patients recover without treatment [N4-F3].

Which patient groups benefit most from corticosteroids? The evidence suggests benefit is strongest in patients who receive treatment early, especially within 72 hours of symptom onset [N6-F4][N4-F3]. The NEJM study specifically found that prednisolone improved recovery at 3 and 9 months, with the most significant benefit when treatment was started early [N3-F2]. The Medscape source also notes that patients treated with prednisolone within 48 hours had significantly higher rates of complete recovery than those treated later [N4-F3]. So the clearest benefit is in early-onset Bell’s palsy, not necessarily in all cases.

Estimated risk reduction for incomplete recovery or severe outcomes is difficult to quantify precisely from the provided evidence, but the NEJM study provides a concrete figure: the relative difference between patients treated with prednisolone and those not treated was 26.6% at 3 months [N3-R3]. In other words, corticosteroids appear to reduce the risk of incomplete recovery or severe outcomes compared with no treatment, though the absolute benefit is moderate and should be interpreted in context. The Medscape source similarly states that steroids are highly likely to be effective and increase the likelihood of recovery of facial nerve function [N4-F3].

Common corticosteroid regimens and duration of use are best supported by the NEJM evidence. The study used prednisolone, and the guideline excerpt recommends 1 mg/kg or 60 mg/day for 6 days [N4-F3]. The NEJM trial also used 10 days of treatment with prednisolone [N3-F2]. The evidence base here is strong enough to support a standard regimen of high-dose corticosteroids started promptly, but the exact duration may vary by protocol. The evidence does not provide a universally agreed “best” regimen beyond the general principle of early initiation and a short course [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Possible harms or side effects to consider are limited in the provided evidence, but the NEJM study reports no serious adverse events in any group [N3-F2]. Medscape notes that corticosteroids are still controversial because most patients recover without treatment, implying that harms may be overestimated in routine practice [N4-F3]. In practice, corticosteroids may cause short-term side effects such as increased appetite, insomnia, or fluid retention, and longer-term use may raise concerns about adrenal suppression or infection risk. However, the evidence provided does not give detailed safety data for Bell’s palsy specifically [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, corticosteroids are helpful in Bell’s palsy, particularly for patients treated early, with the strongest evidence for reducing incomplete recovery and improving facial function [N3-F2][N4-F3][N6-F4]. The benefit is most pronounced when treatment is initiated within 72 hours, and the regimen is typically a short course of high-dose steroids [N4-F3]. The evidence is strongest for corticosteroids alone, not for combination with antivirals, and the harms appear low in the provided studies [N3-F2][N4-F3].

A strong mini-report on antiviral use and combination therapy

Antivirals improve outcomes beyond steroids alone only modestly, and the evidence is mixed. The Medscape reference says antiviral treatment has also come into use, but evidence is now available indicating that it may not be beneficial [N4-F3]. The 2012 AAN guideline says acyclovir (with prednisone) is possibly effective, while the 2012 AAN update states that steroids are highly likely to be effective and antivirals are possibly effective [N4-F3]. The most direct evidence from the provided sources is that acyclovir given alone did not show any significant difference in the rate of facial recovery compared with placebo, and there was no additional benefit from combining acyclovir and prednisolone compared with prednisolone alone [N3-F2]. A later review also found no clinically significant difference between treatment groups in secondary outcomes, further supporting that antivirals alone or in combination with steroids do not add major benefit [N3-F2].

Which antivirals are most commonly used and what is their evidence level? The evidence mentions acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir as the most commonly used antivirals in combination with corticosteroids [N4-R1]. The Medscape reference also lists acyclovir and valacyclovir as antiviral agents considered if a viral etiology is suspected [N4-F3]. However, the evidence level is not uniformly strong. The provided RCT evidence is high quality, but the outcome was not clearly improved by antivirals alone or in combination with steroids [N3-F2]. Medscape therefore states that the evidence is now available indicating that antivirals may not be beneficial [N4-F3], and the search result for combination therapy states that combination therapy may be effective but that no statistically significant differences were observed [N3-R1]. So the best-supported conclusion is that antivirals are commonly used, but their evidence for benefit is weak.

Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is relevant because Bell’s palsy and herpes-related disease can overlap, and the evidence explicitly notes that the facial nerve canal is narrow and that swelling may cause compression and damage [N4-F3]. It also mentions that herpes zoster infection is part of the differential diagnosis, with the physical examination including inspection for herpes zoster [N6-F4]. The Medscape source further notes that antiviral treatment is considered if a viral etiology is suspected [N4-F3]. This is important because Bell’s palsy is not the same as herpes zoster ophthalmicus, and the latter may require more urgent evaluation. The provided evidence does not provide a direct comparison of herpes zoster ophthalmicus versus Bell’s palsy, but it does establish that herpes-related inflammation is a relevant differential and that antivirals may be considered in suspected viral cases [N4-F3][N6-F4].

How does combination therapy compare with steroids alone? The evidence points in two directions. One source says combination therapy may be effective, but no statistically significant differences were observed [N3-R1]. Another says acyclovir given alone did not improve recovery, and combining acyclovir with prednisolone did not add benefit [N3-F2]. Medscape similarly states that steroids are highly likely to be effective and antivirals possibly effective, but no recommendations can be made for acupuncture, physical therapy, electrotherapy, or surgical decompression because well-designed studies are lacking [N4-F3]. The provided evidence therefore suggests that combination therapy is often used, but it is not clearly superior to steroids alone in the best-designed trials, and the benefit may be only modest or non-existent [N3-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

In summary, antivirals are commonly used in Bell’s palsy and are often combined with corticosteroids, but the evidence does not support them as a major additional benefit over steroids alone [N3-F2][N4-F3]. Acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir are the most commonly mentioned antivirals, but their evidence level is weak [N4-R1][N4-F3]. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is a relevant differential because it shares some pathophysiology and may require urgent evaluation [N4-F3][N6-F4]. Combination therapy is used in practice, but the provided evidence does not show it to be clearly better than steroids alone [N3-R1][N3-F2].

A strong mini-report on urgent care and when to refer

Red flags that require urgent evaluation are clearly outlined in the evidence. The RACGP guidance says GPs should refer patients with new or worsening neurological findings, facial diplegia, ocular symptoms or complications, or incomplete facial nerve recovery [N6-F4]. It also notes that associated symptoms of diplopia, dysphagia, genuine numbness of the face or dizziness are not typical of Bell’s palsy and are red flag symptoms suggestive of other diagnoses [N6-F4]. Medscape similarly states that the diagnosis is based on exclusion and that the history should specifically enquire about onset and timing of symptoms [N4-F3]. The StatPearls source reinforces that Bell’s palsy is an acute, idiopathic, unilateral paralysis of the facial nerve and that the exact mechanism is unknown, although a viral aetiology is suspected [N1-R3]. Together, these sources indicate that urgent evaluation is needed when the presentation is not typical Bell’s palsy, when neurological signs develop, or when ocular complications arise.

When to start treatment immediately versus watchful waiting depends on the patient’s presentation and timing. The evidence supports early treatment for Bell’s palsy, especially within 72 hours of symptom onset [N6-F4][N4-F3]. The NEJM study showed that early treatment with prednisolone significantly improved complete recovery at 3 and 9 months, while the Medscape source states that steroids should be started immediately once the decision is made [N4-F3]. However, the evidence also notes that most patients recover without treatment [N4-F3]. So the guidance is not to watch and wait for all patients, but to treat promptly when the condition is acute and suspected to be Bell’s palsy, while avoiding treatment for patients who may be improving spontaneously [N4-F3][N6-F4]. The Medscape reference also says that treatment may be considered for patients who present within 1–4 days of the onset of paralysis, but that treatment is still controversial because spontaneous recovery is common [N4-F3].

Symptoms that signal neurological complications include diplopia, dysphagia, genuine numbness of the face, and dizziness [N6-F4]. These are not typical of Bell’s palsy and should prompt urgent evaluation for stroke, Guillain–Barré syndrome, multiple sclerosis, or other serious diagnoses [N6-F4]. The Medscape source similarly emphasizes the need to exclude stroke, Guillain–Barré syndrome, multiple sclerosis, and other neurological conditions [N4-F3]. Therefore, patients presenting with sudden, severe facial weakness, new neurological signs, or symptoms outside the typical Bell’s palsy picture should not be assumed to be benign and should be evaluated urgently [N6-F4][N4-F3].

What patients should do if recovery does not improve within expected time? The evidence suggests that incomplete recovery is common and that some patients may fail to recover completely [N4-F3][N7-R1]. The StatPearls source notes that 70% to 80% of patients recover completely even without treatment, and over 95% recover with prompt pharmacological therapy [N7-R1]. However, the RACGP guidance says if recovery is not improving after two to three months, a referral to a physiotherapist or speech and language therapist may be appropriate [N6-F4]. The Mayo Clinic also states that there is no one-size-fits-all treatment and that healthcare professionals may suggest medicines or physical therapy to help speed recovery [N5-R1]. The evidence here supports watchful waiting for some patients, but also emphasizes that delayed recovery should prompt specialist evaluation rather than prolonged watchful waiting alone [N6-F4][N7-R1].

Overall, urgent care is needed when the presentation is atypical, neurological signs develop, or ocular complications occur [N6-F4]. Treatment should be started promptly within 72 hours for acute Bell’s palsy, but watchful waiting is not appropriate for all patients [N4-F3][N6-F4]. Symptoms such as diplopia, dysphagia, genuine numbness of the face, or dizziness should signal urgent referral because they may indicate stroke or other serious conditions [N6-F4]. If recovery does not improve within expected time, referral to a specialist or physiotherapy/speech therapy should be considered, rather than continued passive waiting [N6-F4][N7-R1].

# Treatment options for Bell’s palsy in adult patients: steroids helpful?

## Short answer

Yes, **steroids are helpful for Bell’s palsy**, especially when treatment is started **early** — usually within **72 hours of symptom onset**. However, they are **not a guaranteed cure** for everyone, and the best treatment depends on **how soon symptoms start**, whether there are **red flags**, and how well the patient is recovering. **Antivirals** are often used alongside steroids, but the evidence shows they only add **modest benefit** at best. **Eye care, physical therapy, and supportive treatments** can help manage symptoms and prevent complications, but they are not a substitute for corticosteroids when indicated.

## What is Bell’s palsy?

Bell’s palsy is an **acute, unilateral weakness of the facial nerve** without an obvious cause. The evidence suggests that it may result from **facial nerve inflammation and swelling**, and **viral or immune-related causes** are suspected, though the exact mechanism is not fully established [N1-R3][N6-F4]. Most people recover on their own, but some may have incomplete recovery or long-term issues like facial asymmetry, synkinesis, or contractures [N7-R1][N4-F3].

## Are steroids helpful?

### Yes, but the benefit depends on timing
Steroids are the **mainstay of treatment** for Bell’s palsy, and the evidence supports starting them **early**. A large randomized controlled trial showed that **early treatment with prednisolone significantly improved complete recovery** at 3 and 9 months [N3-F2]. The American Academy of Neurology and other guidelines also support corticosteroids as **highly likely to be effective** and recommend starting them within **72 hours of symptom onset** [N6-F4][N4-F3].

### Which patients benefit most?
The evidence suggests that the **strongest benefit is in patients treated early**, especially within **72 hours** [N6-F4][N4-F3]. The NEJM study found that **patients treated with prednisolone within 48 hours had significantly higher rates of complete recovery** than those treated later [N4-F3]. So, steroids are most helpful when the condition is **acute and suspected early**.

### Estimated risk reduction
The evidence provides a concrete estimate: in the NEJM trial, **patients treated with prednisolone had a 26.6% relative improvement** in recovery at 3 months compared with those who were not treated [N3-R3]. In other words, steroids appear to reduce the risk of incomplete recovery or severe outcomes, but the benefit is **moderate** and should be interpreted in context.

### Common corticosteroid regimens
The evidence supports a **short course of high-dose steroids**. The NEJM study used prednisolone and treatment lasted **10 days** [N3-F2]. The guideline excerpt recommends **1 mg/kg or 60 mg/day for 6 days** [N4-F3]. So the general approach is **early, short-term, high-dose corticosteroids**.

### Are there harms or side effects to consider?
The NEJM trial reported **no serious adverse events** in any group [N3-F2]. Medscape notes that corticosteroids are still controversial because most patients recover without treatment, implying that harms may be **overestimated** in routine practice [N4-F3]. In practice, common short-term side effects may include **increased appetite, insomnia, or fluid retention**, and longer-term use may raise concerns about **adrenal suppression or infection risk**. However, the evidence provided does **not give detailed safety data** specific to Bell’s palsy [N3-F2][N4-F3].

## Antiviral use and combination therapy

### Do antivirals improve outcomes beyond steroids alone?
The evidence is **mixed and mostly weak**. Antiviral treatment has come into use, but the evidence now indicates it **may not be beneficial** [N4-F3]. One trial showed that **acyclovir alone did not improve facial recovery compared with placebo**, and combining acyclovir with prednisolone did **not add significant benefit** [N3-F2]. The evidence notes that the facial nerve travels in a narrow canal and that swelling may cause compression and damage [N4-F3]. It also says the physical examination should look for herpes zoster infection [N6-F4]. ### What symptoms signal neurological complications?
Symptoms that signal neurological complications include **diplopia, dysphagia, genuine numbness of the face, and dizziness** [N6-F4]. The Medscape source also emphasizes the need to **exclude stroke, Guillain–Barré syndrome, multiple sclerosis, and other neurological conditions** [N4-F3]. So patients presenting with **sudden, severe facial weakness, new neurological signs, or symptoms outside the typical Bell’s palsy picture** should be evaluated urgently [N6-F4][N4-F3].

The evidence suggests that **incomplete recovery is common** and that some patients may **fail to recover completely** [N4-F3][N7-R1]. ## Prognosis and recovery expectations

### Overall prognosis
Bell’s palsy has an **overall favorable prognosis**, but it is not guaranteed. The evidence suggests that **70% to 80% of patients recover completely even without treatment**, and **over 95% recover with prompt pharmacological therapy** [N7-R1]. The NEJM study also shows that **prednisolone improved recovery at 3 and 9 months** [N3-F2]. So the outlook is generally good, but not perfect.

### What to expect
Most patients notice **clinical improvement within three weeks** [N6-F4]. Some may recover completely, while others may have **facial weakness, synkinesis, or contractures** [N4-F3][N7-R1]. The evidence also notes that **some patients may fail to recover completely** [N4-F3][N7-R1]. So it is important to explain the condition as **generally favorable, but not guaranteed**, and to reassure the patient that **delayed or incomplete recovery may require follow-up** [N7-R1][N6-F4].

## Patient-specific factors that may change management

### Timing of onset
The earlier treatment starts, the better the likely benefit. The evidence supports **starting treatment within 72 hours** [N6-F4][N4-F3]. Delayed treatment may reduce benefit [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### Severity
More severe cases may need earlier or stronger intervention. The evidence suggests that **severe Bell’s palsy** may benefit from **prompt corticosteroid therapy**, and that incomplete recovery is more common in patients who do not receive early treatment [N4-F3][N7-R1].

### Individual risk profile

For adult patients with Bell’s palsy:

# Treatment options for Bell’s palsy in adult patients: steroids helpful?

Yes, **steroids are helpful for Bell’s palsy**, especially when treatment is started **early** — usually within **72 hours of symptom onset**. ## What is Bell’s palsy?

Bell’s palsy is an **acute, unilateral weakness of the facial nerve** without an obvious cause. The evidence suggests that it may result from **facial nerve inflammation and swelling**, and **viral or immune-related causes** are suspected, though the exact mechanism is not fully established [N1-R3][N6-F4]. Most people recover on their own, but some may have incomplete recovery or long-term issues like facial asymmetry, synkinesis, or contractures [N7-R1][N4-F3].

### Yes, but the benefit depends on timing
Steroids are the **mainstay of treatment** for Bell’s palsy, and the evidence supports starting them **early**. A large randomized controlled trial showed that **early treatment with prednisolone significantly improved complete recovery** at 3 and 9 months [N3-F2]. The American Academy of Neurology and other guidelines also support corticosteroids as **highly likely to be effective** and recommend starting them within **72 hours of symptom onset** [N6-F4][N4-F3].

The evidence suggests that the **strongest benefit is in patients treated early**, especially within **72 hours** [N6-F4][N4-F3]. The NEJM study found that **patients treated with prednisolone within 48 hours had significantly higher rates of complete recovery** than those treated later [N4-F3]. So, steroids are most helpful when the condition is **acute and suspected early**.

### Estimated risk reduction
The evidence provides a concrete estimate: in the NEJM trial, **patients treated with prednisolone had a 26.6% relative improvement** in recovery at 3 months compared with those who were not treated [N3-R3]. In other words, steroids appear to reduce the risk of incomplete recovery or severe outcomes, but the benefit is **moderate** and should be interpreted in context.

The evidence supports a **short course of high-dose steroids**. The NEJM study used prednisolone and treatment lasted **10 days** [N3-F2]. The guideline excerpt recommends **1 mg/kg or 60 mg/day for 6 days** [N4-F3]. So the general approach is **early, short-term, high-dose corticosteroids**.

The NEJM trial reported **no serious adverse events** in any group [N3-F2]. In practice, common short-term side effects may include **increased appetite, insomnia, or fluid retention**, and longer-term use may raise concerns about **adrenal suppression or infection risk**. The American Academy of Neurology and other guidelines also support corticosteroids as **highly likely to be effective** and recommend starting them within **72 hours of symptom onset** [N6-F4][N4-F3].

### Which patients benefit most?
The evidence suggests that the **strongest benefit is in patients treated early**, especially within **72 hours** [N6-F4][N4-F3]. The NEJM study found that **patients treated with prednisolone within 48 hours had significantly higher rates of complete recovery** than those treated later [N4-F3]. So, steroids are most helpful when the condition is **acute and suspected early**.

### Estimated risk reduction
The evidence provides a concrete estimate: in the NEJM trial, **patients treated with prednisolone had a 26.6% relative improvement** in recovery at 3 months compared with those who were not treated [N3-R3]. In other words, steroids appear to reduce the risk of incomplete recovery or severe outcomes, but the benefit is **moderate** and should be interpreted in context.

### Common corticosteroid regimens
The evidence supports a **short course of high-dose steroids**. The NEJM study used prednisolone and treatment lasted **10 days** [N3-F2]. The guideline excerpt recommends **1 mg/kg or 60 mg/day for 6 days** [N4-F3]. So the general approach is **early, short-term, high-dose corticosteroids**.

### Are there harms or side effects to consider?
The NEJM trial reported **no serious adverse events** in any group [N3-F2]. Medscape notes that corticosteroids are still controversial because most patients recover without treatment, implying that harms may be **overestimated** in routine practice [N4-F3]. In practice, common short-term side effects may include **increased appetite, insomnia, or fluid retention**, and longer-term use may raise concerns about **adrenal suppression or infection risk**. However, the evidence provided does **not give detailed safety data** specific to Bell’s palsy [N3-F2][N4-F3].

## Antiviral use and combination therapy

### Do antivirals improve outcomes beyond steroids alone?
The evidence is **mixed and mostly weak**. Antiviral treatment has come into use, but the evidence now indicates it **may not be beneficial** [N4-F3]. One trial showed that **acyclovir alone did not improve facial recovery compared with placebo**, and combining acyclovir with prednisolone did **not add significant benefit** [N3-F2]. Another source says combination therapy may be effective, but **no statistically significant differences were observed** [N3-R1].

### Which antivirals are most commonly used?
The evidence mentions **acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir** as the most commonly used antivirals in combination with corticosteroids [N4-R1]. The Medscape reference also lists **acyclovir and valacyclovir** as agents considered if a viral etiology is suspected [N4-F3]. However, the evidence level is **weak** for benefit beyond steroids alone [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### When is herpes zoster ophthalmicus relevant?
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is **relevant because Bell’s palsy and herpes-related disease can overlap**. The evidence notes that the facial nerve travels in a narrow canal and that swelling may cause compression and damage [N4-F3]. It also says the physical examination should look for herpes zoster infection [N6-F4]. So if a patient has **atypical symptoms** or signs of **herpes infection**, urgent evaluation is needed, but Bell’s palsy itself is not the same as herpes zoster ophthalmicus [N4-F3][N6-F4].

### How does combination therapy compare with steroids alone?
Combination therapy is often used, but the evidence does **not show clear superiority** over steroids alone. One source says combination therapy may be effective, but **no statistically significant differences were observed** [N3-R1]. Another says **acyclovir alone did not improve recovery**, and adding acyclovir to steroids did not add benefit [N3-F2]. Medscape similarly says steroids are highly likely to be effective and antivirals possibly effective, but it does **not recommend** acupuncture, physical therapy, electrotherapy, or surgical decompression because the evidence is weak [N4-F3]. So the best-supported conclusion is that **combination therapy may be used, but the benefit is only modest or uncertain** [N3-F2][N3-R1][N4-F3].

## Eye care, physical therapy, and supportive treatments

### Eye protection, eye drops, and artificial tears
Eye care is central to Bell’s palsy because the condition often causes **incomplete eye closure**. The evidence says **eye care is essential for patients with incomplete eye closure** and that topical ocular therapy is useful in most cases, with exceptions for **severe or prolonged disease** [N4-F3]. Medical News Today explains how to use eye drops and eye-care strategies during recovery [N5-R4]. The Mayo Clinic also notes that healthcare professionals may suggest eye drops as part of treatment [N5-R1]. These treatments help **protect the cornea and reduce complications**, but they are **not a substitute for corticosteroids or antivirals** when indicated [N4-F3][N5-R4].

### Facial massage, physical therapy, and massage therapy
Physical therapy is part of the supportive care bundle. The Mayo Clinic says healthcare professionals may suggest **medicines or physical therapy** to help speed recovery [N5-R1]. Medscape lists **facial exercises, neuromuscular retraining**, and other nonpharmacologic measures, and notes that many issues such as eating, drinking, swallowing, and speech disturbance may be addressed with **occupational therapy and speech therapy** [N4-F3]. The evidence suggests physical therapy may help **speed recovery and reduce sequelae**, but further randomized, controlled trials are needed to confirm any benefit [N4-F3].

### Acupuncture and non-invasive therapies
Acupuncture is mentioned as an option, but the evidence is **thin**. Medscape says **no adverse effects** have been reported, but it also notes that reviews suggest physical therapy may help and that more evidence is needed [N4-F3]. The search evidence also says corticosteroids, antiviral drugs, physical therapy, and supportive measures are available treatment alternatives [N5-R3]. So acupuncture should be framed as an **adjunct or complementary option**, not a first-line treatment [N4-F3][N5-R3].

### How these treatments fit into recovery
These supportive treatments fit into recovery as part of a **broader management plan**. Eye care is prioritized for incomplete eye closure [N4-F3], physical therapy may help speed recovery and reduce sequelae [N4-F3], and non-invasive therapies such as acupuncture may be considered cautiously [N4-F3]. Overall, they are **supportive, not replacement** for corticosteroids or antivirals in the main therapeutic algorithm [N4-F3][N5-R4].

## When to seek urgent care versus watchful waiting

### Red flags that require urgent evaluation
The evidence clearly outlines **red flags** that require urgent evaluation. The RACGP guidance says GPs should refer patients with **new or worsening neurological findings, facial diplegia, ocular symptoms or complications, or incomplete facial nerve recovery** [N6-F4]. It also notes that **diplopia, dysphagia, genuine numbness of the face, or dizziness** are not typical of Bell’s palsy and are **red flag symptoms suggestive of other diagnoses** [N6-F4]. Medscape similarly emphasizes that the diagnosis is based on exclusion and that the history should specifically ask about **onset and timing of symptoms** [N4-F3].

### When to start treatment immediately versus watchful waiting
The evidence supports **prompt treatment for Bell’s palsy**, especially within **72 hours of symptom onset** [N6-F4][N4-F3]. The NEJM study showed that early treatment with prednisolone significantly improved complete recovery at 3 and 9 months, while the Medscape source says steroids should be started immediately once the decision is made [N4-F3]. However, the evidence also notes that **most patients recover without treatment** [N4-F3]. So the practical guidance is not to **watch and wait for all patients**, but to treat **promptly when the condition is acute and suspected to be Bell’s palsy** [N4-F3][N6-F4].

### What symptoms signal neurological complications?
Symptoms that signal neurological complications include **diplopia, dysphagia, genuine numbness of the face, and dizziness** [N6-F4]. These are **not typical of Bell’s palsy** and may indicate **stroke, Guillain–Barré syndrome, multiple sclerosis, or other serious conditions** [N6-F4]. The Medscape source also emphasizes the need to **exclude stroke, Guillain–Barré syndrome, multiple sclerosis, and other neurological conditions** [N4-F3]. So patients presenting with **sudden, severe facial weakness, new neurological signs, or symptoms outside the typical Bell’s palsy picture** should be evaluated urgently [N6-F4][N4-F3].

### What to do if recovery does not improve within expected time
The evidence suggests that **incomplete recovery is common** and that some patients may **fail to recover completely** [N4-F3][N7-R1]. StatPearls notes that **70% to 80% of patients recover completely even without treatment**, and **over 95% recover with prompt pharmacological therapy** [N7-R1]. However, the RACGP guidance says if recovery is not improving after **two to three months**, a referral to a **physiotherapist or speech and language therapist** may be appropriate [N6-F4]. So the message is: **watch carefully for delayed recovery, but do not delay specialist follow-up** [N6-F4][N7-R1].

## Prognosis and recovery expectations

### Overall prognosis
Bell’s palsy has an **overall favorable prognosis**, but it is not guaranteed. The evidence suggests that **70% to 80% of patients recover completely even without treatment**, and **over 95% recover with prompt pharmacological therapy** [N7-R1]. The NEJM study also shows that **prednisolone improved recovery at 3 and 9 months** [N3-F2]. So the outlook is generally good, but not perfect.

### What to expect
Most patients notice **clinical improvement within three weeks** [N6-F4]. Some may recover completely, while others may have **facial weakness, synkinesis, or contractures** [N4-F3][N7-R1]. The evidence also notes that **some patients may fail to recover completely** [N4-F3][N7-R1]. So it is important to explain the condition as **generally favorable, but not guaranteed**, and to reassure the patient that **delayed or incomplete recovery may require follow-up** [N7-R1][N6-F4].

## Patient-specific factors that may change management

### Timing of onset
The earlier treatment starts, the better the likely benefit. The evidence supports **starting treatment within 72 hours** [N6-F4][N4-F3]. Delayed treatment may reduce benefit [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### Severity
More severe cases may need earlier or stronger intervention. The evidence suggests that **severe Bell’s palsy** may benefit from **prompt corticosteroid therapy**, and that incomplete recovery is more common in patients who do not receive early treatment [N4-F3][N7-R1].

### Individual risk profile
The evidence notes that risk factors include **pregnancy, severe pre-eclampsia, obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and upper respiratory illnesses such as influenza** [N6-F4]. These factors do not change the core treatment algorithm, but they may influence the urgency of evaluation and the choice of supportive measures.

### Management should be guided by severity and probable prognosis
The Medscape source emphasizes that management should be **conservative and guided by severity and probable prognosis in each case** [N4-F3]. So the best approach is to **treat promptly when Bell’s palsy is suspected**, watch for red flags, and adjust care based on individual response and timing [N4-F3][N6-F4].

## Bottom line

For adult patients with Bell’s palsy:

- **Steroids are helpful**, especially when started **within 72 hours** of symptom onset [N6-F4][N4-F3].
- **Early treatment improves recovery** at 3 and 9 months, but not all patients recover completely [N3-F2][N7-R1].
- **Antivirals may be used**, but the evidence shows they only add **modest benefit at best** [N4-F3][N3-F2].
- **Eye care is essential** for incomplete eye closure, and **physical therapy may help** with recovery and sequelae [N4-F3][N5-R1].
- **Watch for red flags** such as neurological signs, diplopia, dysphagia, or incomplete recovery — these may signal serious complications [N6-F4][N4-F3].
- **If recovery does not improve within expected time**, specialist follow-up is appropriate [N6-F4][N7-R1].

So, steroids are **helpful in Bell’s palsy**, but the best treatment depends on **how soon symptoms start**, whether there are **red flags**, and how the patient responds to treatment.
